There's a neat algorithmic way to accomplish this. Simply consider each CCP a "ticket" in the selection pool. Once somebody is selected, the entirety of the CCP they had accounted for during the last mod-cycle is removed during the next cycle.

So 3 people start with 50, 30 and 20 CCP. Since the total CCP in the pool is 100, the person with 50 CCP would have a 50/100 or 50% chance of being selected followed by the 30% and the 20% for the other two people. Let's say the 50% guy wins. In the month that passes he and the other 2 accounts gain 10 CCP each. In the next wave the same 3 people would have (60-50), 40 and 30 CCP. Since the total is 80 the first guy would have a 10/80 or 12.5% chance "winning" again, followed by 50% and 37.5%.

In the longrun you'd mostly have people that are active and contributing to the sub but most anybody could potentially become a mod.

Bowyer here...building a survival bow stems from a misunderstanding of the principles of bow building.

You don't need to build a survival bow. By that I mean that it can be improvised in 20 min. Wouldn't really call that building.

The reason people spent good time and effort in building bows is for reliability/longevity and efficiency.

A few pointers:

branches are naturally tapered. You can cut off a branch and attach strings. It will shoot. The reason that is unintuitive is because the bow will be very asymmetrical. It looks like shit.

or get two comparable, tapered branches.

Attach them by the thick ends with the handle area overlapping.

straight branches can be bundled. Let's say you have 5 branches of the same diameter. You string or tape them together. 5 branches intact in the middle. Cut off one of the branches at both ends 10 inches from the center. Continue cutting off branches in even intervals. At the tips of the limbs, you only have a single branch remaining. If you get access to bamboo, you're set. A bamboo bow like that will be nicer than the bow in the video.

green wood is more resistant to breaking. That's why we can use absurd designs.

length is everything. Sure, a 55" bow is what people are used to from commercial hunting bows but increase the length to above 70" and you will see how hard it becomes to break bows.

performance of bows is least important. The difference between the worst bush bow and one made with choice materials in a workshop is negligible. You'd be surprised if you saw what bows native Americans used. But they still killed.

to add onto the last point, you can always compensate for efficiency. For example, you can increase the poundage. Even the worst bush bow that reaches 50 lbs and full draw will be effective enough for hunting. Heavy arrows will improve a bow's efficiency as well.
